stem: A client who is 24 weeks pregnant receives a new prescription for oral tetracycline. Which action is most appropriate before the first dose?

options.A: Administer the tetracycline because the fetal tooth-development warning applies mainly to first-trimester exposure and is not relevant after 20 weeks of pregnancy.
options.B: Administer the prescribed short course because permanent tooth discoloration has been associated with prolonged therapy rather than repeated short-term tetracycline exposure.
options.C: Administer the tetracycline with a calcium-containing meal so intestinal binding reduces fetal exposure enough to address the tooth-development warning during pregnancy.
options.D: Hold the first dose and clarify the prescription because 24 weeks is within the last half of pregnancy, when tetracycline-class exposure can permanently discolor developing teeth.

rationale: Current DailyMed tetracycline hydrochloride labeling warns that use of tetracycline-class drugs during tooth development, including the last half of pregnancy, may cause permanent yellow-gray-brown discoloration of developing teeth and that enamel hypoplasia has also been reported. The labeling notes that this adverse effect is more common with long-term use but has also occurred after repeated short-term courses and states that tetracyclines should not be used during this period except in specified circumstances when other drugs are not likely to be effective or are contraindicated. A client at 24 weeks is within the last half of pregnancy, so the nurse should hold the first dose and clarify the prescription rather than assume the exception applies. D is therefore correct. A reverses the timing of the warning. B incorrectly treats short-course exposure as exempt from the tooth-development concern. C does not address the fetal risk and calcium can reduce tetracycline absorption rather than serve as a fetal-protection strategy.
educational_objective: Recognize the last half of pregnancy as a tetracycline tooth-development risk period and clarify a new tetracycline prescription before administration rather than assuming short duration or altered administration removes the fetal risk.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
source_document_title: Tetracycline Hydrochloride Capsules, USP — Prescribing Information
source_version_date: Current DailyMed label dated May 22, 2026; accessed 2026-08-25
source_locator: Warnings > Tooth Development: use of tetracycline-class drugs during tooth development, including the last half of pregnancy, may cause permanent yellow-gray-brown tooth discoloration; the reaction is more common during long-term use but has been observed following repeated short-term courses; enamel hypoplasia has also been reported; tetracycline drugs should not be used during this period except for anthrax unless other drugs are not likely to be effective or are contraindicated. Drug Interactions/administration information: absorption of tetracyclines is impaired by antacids containing calcium and by iron-containing preparations, so calcium binding is not a strategy to neutralize fetal risk.
source_claim_supported: Tetracycline-class exposure during the last half of pregnancy can permanently discolor developing teeth and may cause enamel hypoplasia; short-course exposure is not categorically exempt, so a new prescription at 24 weeks warrants clarification before administration unless a justified exception is confirmed.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 12: evaluate appropriateness and accuracy of medication orders; review pertinent data prior to medication administration, including contraindications and potential interactions; educate clients about medications; evaluate client response. Related Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions content includes identifying contraindications and notifying the primary health care provider of medication contraindications or adverse-effect concerns.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — pregnancy-related medication risk and prescription clarification
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to remove distractor-only absolute wording and replace simplistic errors with realistic misconceptions about trimester timing, short-course exposure, and calcium coadministration. The keyed action preserves the label's exception language by requiring clarification rather than declaring tetracycline universally prohibited in pregnancy.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Tetracycline medication safety — pregnancy and fetal tooth development
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies 24 weeks of pregnancy and a new oral tetracycline prescription, making the label's last-half-of-pregnancy warning directly applicable without assuming the infection or indication.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — first-trimester teratogenicity is a familiar medication concern, but tetracycline labeling specifically identifies the last half of pregnancy for tooth-development risk.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — shorter antibiotic courses may seem safer, but the label explicitly notes permanent discoloration has occurred after repeated short-term courses and does not exempt a new short course from review.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — calcium-tetracycline binding is real pharmacology, but it reduces drug absorption and is not a recommended method for preventing fetal tooth effects.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS — directly applies the current tooth-development warning while appropriately asking the prescriber to confirm whether a labeled exception or alternative applies; uniquely best.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — D is the only option that recognizes the correct gestational risk period without inventing a duration exemption or an administration workaround.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A misstates timing, B creates an unsupported short-course exemption, and C substitutes reduced absorption for clinical risk assessment.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all alternatives are comparable in length and clinical detail and no distractor-only absolute term remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly includes medication-order appropriateness, contraindication review, interactions, and provider notification.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether tetracycline should simply be labeled absolutely contraindicated at 24 weeks. Current labeling retains exceptions when other drugs are unlikely to be effective or are contraindicated, so the final answer correctly uses hold-and-clarify rather than a universal prohibition while still recognizing the directly sourced fetal tooth-development risk. D remains uniquely best.
